cards.title: 8 Pakistan Bar Council members call on judiciary to take note of Imran's plea for medical treatment
cards.author: Nasir Iqbal, News Desk
cards.why: This case involves constitutional rights, the independence of the judiciary, and the executive's adherence to Supreme Court directives, all of which are essential topics for Pakistan Affairs and Governance.
cards.summary: Eight Pakistan Bar Council members have formally petitioned the judiciary to enforce a Supreme Court order for the medical treatment of former PM Imran Khan. The request follows reports that the government failed to move him to Shifa International Hospital as mandated. The legal group emphasized that ensuring a fair trial and medical care is a constitutional obligation.
key_facts: A three-member Supreme Court bench ordered Imran Khan to be moved to Shifa International Hospital on Aug 18.
The petition was signed by eight members of the Pakistan Bar Council.
The signatories include prominent legal figures such as Abid Shahid Zuberi and Salman Akram Raja.
The plea highlights the constitutional requirement for fair trial and due process for all incarcerated individuals.
text: ISLAMABAD: Eight members of the Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) on Tuesday called upon the judiciary to ensure implementation of the Supreme Court’s (SC) order directing incarcerated ex-premier Imran Khan’s transfer to Shifa International Hospital for medical treatment.

On Aug 18 , a three-member SC bench had directed the government to shift Imran to SIH within the next two days as it heard several petitions concerning his health. However, the government took the PTI founder to the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences for a check-up and then transported him back to prison.

On Monday, in an open letter to the chief justices of the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), the SC and the Islamabad High Court (IHC), Imran appealed for medical treatment for himself and Bushra Bibi. He also said that he would only be able to prove his innocence in the various cases against him “if I stay alive”.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, eight members of the PBC said: “We call upon the judiciary to take up the former prime minister’s plea immediately and to save his and his wife’s lives by ensuring that court orders are implemented, that proper medical treatment is provided and that due process and a fair trial are guaranteed as mandated by the Constitution.”
The statement was signed by Abid Shahid Zuberi, Muhammad Maqsood Buttar, Shafqat Mehmood Chauhan, Abdul Sattar Khan, Munir Ahmed Kakar, Salman Akram Raja, Salahuddin Ahmed and Qazi Muhammad Arshad.

The PBC members urged the government and its agencies to implement court orders and ensure that both Imran and his wife received proper medical treatment in accordance with the law and the Constitution. The statement warned that the government and its agencies would be solely responsible for “imperilling” the lives and liberty of the couple.
“We the undersigned reserve our right to initiate legal proceedings to protect the life, liberty, and constitutional and legal rights of Imran and Bushra Bibi,” the statement said.

The statement also condemned “in the strongest terms” the alleged unlawful and unconstitutional treatment meted out to Imran and his wife, adding that the situation was endangering their lives, liberty and dignity.

“[Imran’s] letter reveals that the former prime minister and his wife have been denied their constitutional and human rights through trumped-up and false cases and that they are incarcerated in violation of the law, the jail manual and the prison rules,” the statement asserted.
The statement further added that Imran and Bushra Bibi were convicted in false cases and their appeals against these convictions had not been heard.
“Even their bail applications have not been fixed for hearing,” it said.

The statement further highlighted that Imran had been kept in solitary confinement and denied due medical treatment and access to his legal team and family members, jeopardising his and his wife’s health.

The statement also alleged that his sisters had been detained arbitrarily and unlawfully, while the SC’s Aug 18 order had been openly flouted by the government and its agencies in violation of the law and the Constitution.
“Every person in Pakistan is guaranteed the right to life and liberty under Article 9, and the right to due process and a fair trial under Article 10-A of the Constitution,” the statement said.
“These rights have been denied to Imran, his wife, his family and his party members,” it said.

“As patriotic Pakistanis who believe in the rule of law, we are ashamed to read Imran’s plea for implementation of the SC’s orders and for the proper medical treatment that has been denied to him and his wife,” the statement said.

Moreover, the Democratic Alliance, a confederation of lawyers led by former PBC vice chairman Abid Saqi, expressed grave alarm over what it described as the deteriorating health and unlawful detention conditions of Imran and his family members.
In a statement, the alliance asked the judiciary to take immediate notice of the matter and enforce its orders concerning medical treatment and access to family members.
It also called on the government to end Imran’s solitary confinement, provide him with comprehensive medical treatment and release family members held without cause.
The alliance’s statement further urged the international community and human rights organisations to take urgent cognisance of the “grave” situation.

“The life of a former prime minister and his family hang in the balance. Justice delayed is justice denied. The Democratic Alliance demands that the rule of law and human dignity prevail before it is too late,” the statement said.
HRCP, Amnesty express concern

Separately, the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan also expressed “deep concern” at what it called the state’s treatment of political prisoners, urging authorities to uphold their fundamental rights, irrespective of political affiliation.
Referring to the allegations Imran made in his letter, the HRCP said they required urgent and independent examination.

“HRCP stresses that violations of political prisoners’ fundamental freedoms are not a matter of personalities or political affiliations; they constitute an assault on the rule of law,” the commission said.

“Every prisoner is entitled to humane treatment, adequate healthcare, access to family and lawyers, and a fair trial. All relevant court orders must be implemented and allegations of mistreatment independently investigated,” it added.

Meanwhile, Amnesty International said the “persistent denial of adequate health care, family visits, and regular meetings with legal counsel” to Imran and Bushra were a “violation of Pakistan’s international human rights obligations”.

Narrating complaints made by the former premier about the treatment allegedly meted out to him and his wife, Amnesty said, “In denying Imran Khan and Bushra Bibi their rights, the Pakistani authorities run afoul their international law commitments.

“Article 10 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which Pakistan is a state party, guarantees that any person denied of their liberty ‘shall be treated with humanity and with respect’,” it pointed out.
Amnesty urged the authorities to “immediately provide adequate healthcare to Imran Khan and Bushra Bibi and restore regular access to family and lawyers”.

Recalling the detentions of Imran’s sisters, Amnesty contended that his family “has also been targeted”. While two of his sisters were released last week, Aleema Khan remains under detention in Kot Lakhpat prison, it noted.

“Political persecution of Imran Khan’s family, particularly of his sisters for advocating for his rights, must stop. This includes the immediate release of Aleema Khan, and the authorities must ensure that no further charges are brought against family members for exercising their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly,” Amnesty stated.

cards.title: US proposes tougher rules for employment-based green cards
cards.author: Anwar Iqbal
cards.why: This is a critical update on international migration policies and global labor market trends, which are relevant to the Globalization and International Relations components of the syllabus.
cards.summary: The US Department of Labor has proposed stricter rules for employment-based green cards to prioritize American workers. The changes include extending recruitment periods from 30 to 90 days and restricting companies that have recently conducted layoffs from sponsoring foreign talent. These measures aim to protect domestic wages and ensure fair consideration of American applicants.
key_facts: The proposed rules affect EB-2 and EB-3 green card categories under the PERM programme.
The minimum mandatory recruitment period for employers will increase from 30 to 90 days.
Employers are now required to disclose salary ranges in job advertisements.
Companies that have recently laid off American workers will face restricted ability to sponsor foreign employees.

vocab.meaning: In a way that prevents success or development; harmfully.

text: WASHINGTON: The United States Department of Labour has published sweeping proposed changes to the rules governing employment-based green cards, requiring companies to make greater efforts to recruit American workers before sponsoring foreign employees for permanent residency.

The proposed overhaul would extend recruitment periods, restrict sponsorship by companies that have recently laid off US workers and eliminate special exemptions currently available to certain healthcare professionals.

Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling said existing rules had allowed companies to sponsor foreign workers “without fully considering American applicants”, a practice the department seeks to address through “expanded recruitment and enforcement requirements”.
The proposals would affect employers seeking to sponsor foreign nationals through the EB-2 and EB-3 employment-based green card categories under the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme.

Under the existing system , employers must demonstrate that qualified American workers are unavailable for a particular position and that hiring a foreign worker would not adversely affect domestic wages or working conditions.

The proposed rules would increase the minimum recruitment period from 30 to 90 calendar days. Employers that normally advertise comparable vacancies for longer periods would be required to follow their established recruitment schedules.

Companies would also have to expand their use of digital recruitment platforms, including online job boards, corporate websites and social media. Job advertisements would be required to disclose offered wages or salary ranges, while employers would have to demonstrate that American applicants received fair consideration.

Employers would face stricter documentation requirements as well. They would have to submit recruitment reports, supporting records and the resumes of American applicants along with their labour certification applications. Under current regulations, much of this material is generally retained by employers and produced if an application is selected for a federal audit.

Another significant provision would restrict companies that have laid off American workers in the same or similar occupations within the same geographical area during the preceding two years from obtaining labour certification for those positions.

Existing regulations generally require employers to notify and consider potentially qualified American workers laid off within the previous six months. The proposed changes would extend the period during which such layoffs could affect sponsorship decisions.

The restrictions would also cover certain layoffs involving third-party staffing companies. Employers would have to report subsequent workforce reductions and continue considering qualified displaced American workers during the related immigration petition process.
Healthcare employers could face additional difficulties under the proposed overhaul.

The department plans to eliminate Schedule A, a provision that currently allows employers to sponsor professional nurses, physical therapists and certain individuals with exceptional abilities in the sciences or arts without completing the standard labour market recruitment process.

Removing the exemption would require hospitals and other healthcare facilities to advertise vacancies, consider qualified American applicants and obtain labour certification before proceeding with immigration petitions for foreign professionals.
The change could particularly affect healthcare institutions that rely on internationally recruited nurses and physical therapists.
The proposals would constitute the first comprehensive overhaul of PERM regulations in nearly two decades.

cards.title: UK sanctions Israeli firms helping build West Bank settlements
cards.author: AFP
cards.why: This story relates to the Israel-Palestine conflict, international law, and human rights, which are key themes in Current Affairs and International Relations.
cards.summary: The UK government has sanctioned eight Israeli construction and property firms involved in West Bank settlement expansion. The policy aims to discourage further development in occupied territories and protect the viability of a two-state solution. Britain also expressed concern regarding the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, citing obstacles to essential shelter materials.
key_facts: Sanctions were imposed on eight Israeli construction and property development firms.
The UN has previously stated that projects in the E1 area pose an existential threat to a contiguous Palestinian state.
The UK Foreign Office reported that 150,000 tents and 300,000 tarpaulins meant for Gaza are being held by Israeli authorities.
According to the Foreign Office, 1.4 million people in Gaza are currently living in makeshift shelters.

vocab.meaning: Relating to existence; posing a threat to the survival of something.

text: Britain on Tuesday announced a slew of sanctions against eight Israeli companies helping to plan and build West Bank settlements, in a bid to halt new construction.
“Do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution,” foreign minister Ed Miliband urged Israeli companies.
European leaders have already condemned plans to construct more than 1,200 homes in the occupied West Bank which were put out to tender in August.
And the UN secretary general has said the E1 project posed an “existential threat” to a contiguous Palestinian state.
The UK’s Foreign Office said Tuesday’s “sanctions target construction and property development firms involved in settlement expansion”.

“The UK has taken firm action against eight construction and property development firms which will disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support further construction in the West Bank,” it added in a statement.
The move comes amid heavy criticism of Israel for blocking desperately needed supplies of tents and timber into the devastated Gaza Strip which has been hit by heavy flooding.

Heavy rain earlier this month swept away tens of thousands of tents in the ravaged Palestinian territory, where virtually the entire population has been displaced at least once, according to Hamas-led authorities in Gaza.

The Foreign Office, citing the UN, said “over 150,000 tents and 300,000 tarpaulins that humanitarian partners and donors purchased are outside Gaza ready to go in but are being held by the Israeli authorities”.
It said the floods had led to “nearly 4,000 households left without shelter and 1.4 million people living in tents or makeshift shelters”.
And it accused Israeli authorities of blocking “timber from entering, leaving no emergency shelter kits available in Gaza”.
The UK’s Foreign Office also sanctioned Israeli activist group Tzav 9 on Tuesday for blocking aid deliveries into Gaza.
“We will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza,” Miliband said.
The sanctions result in asset freezes for the companies and group as well as director disqualifications.
One of the blacklisted Israeli companies, real estate developer Harey Zahav, sparked controversy in 2023 when it posted a slogan on social media voicing hopes of returning settlers to Gaza.
It has gained a reputation for constructing wildcat settler outposts in the occupied West Bank without Israeli government authorisation.

cards.title: PTA finalises licensing framework for 'sky-high' internet, telecommunication services
cards.author: News Desk
cards.why: This development represents a shift in national digital infrastructure and regulatory governance in the aviation sector.
cards.summary: The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority has finalized a framework for satellite-based in-flight internet and telecommunication services. This regulation allows Pakistani-registered aircraft to offer connectivity through authorized satellite providers. Transit aircraft using Pakistani airspace will require specific no-objection certificates to utilize these digital services.
key_facts: The framework authorizes satellite-based connectivity for Pakistani-registered aircraft.
Providers must register with the Pakistan Space Activities Regulatory Board.
Compliance with PTA licensing requirements is mandatory for all participating operators.
Transit aircraft must obtain an NOC from the authority to operate within Pakistani airspace.

vocab.meaning: Relating to the earth or land; not satellite-based.
